pos: n. phr. (the Song's great declaration on the strength of covenant love)
etymology: Hebrew azzah ka-mavet ahabah — az, strong, fierce, unyielding; mavet, death; ahabah, love; the comparison is not of sweetness but of grip, death being the one power nothing escapes.
biblical_def: “Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.” The comparison the Song chooses is startling and deliberate. Death is not praised for beauty; it is feared for its hold — it takes what it takes and does not give back. Love, says the bride, has that kind of grip. Three further strokes fill out the figure. The seal is a mark of ownership pressed into wax or worn on the hand, so the request is to be owned and openly claimed. Jealousy here is not the vice but the rightful fierceness of exclusive covenant love, the same word Scripture uses of God's own jealousy for His people. And the coals name its burning: a flame that the Hebrew ties to the LORD's own name. The Song is Solomon's, the canonical celebration of marriage between one man and one woman, and the Reformed have always read it at two levels without confusing them — the literal marriage it plainly describes and commends, and the covenant love of Christ for His church which marriage was made to picture. On either level the sentence stands: this love holds like the grave, and the apostle says that nothing shall separate us from it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Strong, having physical active power; firm; not easily broken or subdued. Love, an affection of the mind excited by beauty and worth. Love is strong as death, Song of Solomon 8:6, the unyielding grip of covenant love.
webster_full: Strong, having active power or force; firm; not easily broken or overcome.
Love, an affection of the mind excited by beauty, worth, or kindness.

Hebrew qin'ah, jealousy or zeal; used of God's own jealousy for His people.
Hebrew chotham, a seal, the mark of ownership pressed or worn.

corruption_summary: The verse is lifted into wedding sentiment with the jealousy and the exclusiveness cut out, and from the other side the Song is reduced to an anthology of unconnected poems with no Solomonic voice and no covenant doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: Engraved on rings and read at weddings, the sentence is now chiefly heard as a compliment to romantic feeling — and the two clauses that make it bite are regularly omitted. The bride asks to be sealed, which is to be owned, and she names jealousy as cruel as the grave, which is the fierce exclusiveness of a covenant that admits no third party. A love strong as death is by definition a love that cannot be shared out or renegotiated, so the verse is the enemy of every arrangement that keeps marriage provisional. Preached whole, it commends what our age will not have: permanence, possession, and a jealousy that is a virtue.

The critical treatment errs in the other direction, dissolving the Song into a collection of unrelated love lyrics gathered late and bearing no single authorial voice, which conveniently removes both its Solomonic attribution and any covenant theology in it. The book names its author in its first verse, the canon has received it as Solomon's, and its movement from courtship to consummation to this closing seal is coherent. The principle to recover is the one the Reformed have held: the Song is literally about marriage and typically about Christ and His church, and a reading that denies either its unity or its Author leaves the church without the only book of Scripture given wholly to the love of husband and wife.

pos: n. phr. (the Song's declaration that covenant love cannot be drowned or bought)
etymology: Hebrew mayim rabbim lo yukhlu le-khabboth et ha-ahabah — mayim rabbim, many or great waters, the standing figure of overwhelming trouble; kabah, to quench or extinguish, properly of putting out a fire.
biblical_def: “Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.” The verse completes the figure begun in the one before it, where love is a flame with coals of fire; now the flame is set against water, and the water loses. Many waters is a biblical idiom for overwhelming calamity — the psalmist is drawn out of many waters, the floods lift up their voice — so the claim is that no weight of trouble can put this fire out. The second half closes the other door. If trouble cannot destroy covenant love, neither can money purchase it; a man who offered his whole estate for it would be despised for the attempt, because love of this kind is not a commodity and the offer insults it. Both halves are true of marriage, which is the Song's subject, and both are true in the higher sense of Christ's love for His church, which neither tribulation nor distress nor persecution nor famine could quench, and which no man purchased — the church is bought, but by blood and not by substance. The two sentences together are the strongest words Scripture gives to the permanence of covenant love.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Quench, to extinguish; to put out, as fire. Flood, a great flow of water; an inundation; a deluge. Many waters cannot quench love, Song of Solomon 8:7, the fire of covenant love neither drowned nor bought.

corruption_summary: Read as a promise that romantic feeling survives anything, the verse becomes a false comfort; and its second half, which despises the purchase of love, is almost always dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: In popular use the sentence becomes a guarantee attaching to feeling: whatever comes, the romance will hold. The Song is not speaking of feeling but of covenant love sealed and owned, and the surrounding book is full of effort — seeking, watching, calling, opening. A couple told that their affection is indestructible by nature has been given a comfort Scripture never offered and will be disillusioned by the first flood. What the verse promises is the nature of covenant love, and the vows of marriage are the form in which two sinners bind themselves to it.

The verse's second clause has nearly vanished from quotation, and it is the sharper of the two: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned. Love is not for sale, and the attempt to buy it earns contempt. That cuts against every arrangement in which affection is traded for advantage — and against the sentimental commerce a wedding industry makes of it. The principle to recover is the apostle's: the love that cannot be quenched is first God's love to us, demonstrated while we were yet sinners and not purchased by anything in us, and human covenant love is strong in the measure that it images that.

pos: n. phr. (the bridegroom's figure for the bride, a spring of running water)
etymology: Hebrew be'er mayim chayyim — be'er, a dug well or pit; mayim chayyim, living waters, the Hebrew term for water that runs and is not stagnant, required for certain purifications in the law.
biblical_def: The bridegroom praises his bride in a run of three figures: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon.” The phrase before it — a garden inclosed, a spring shut up, a fountain sealed — has just named her exclusiveness; now the same water is named for its quality. Living water in Hebrew usage is not a metaphor for vitality in general but a technical description: water that moves, fed from a source, as distinguished from the still water of a cistern. The law required running water for the cleansing of the leper and for the water of separation, so the phrase carries the sense of water fit for purifying. Three things follow. The bride is a source and not a reservoir; her waters are her husband's and sealed to him; and what comes from her is fresh and cleansing rather than kept and stagnant. Scripture takes up the same figure elsewhere and raises it. The LORD indicts His people for forsaking Him, the fountain of living waters, to hew out broken cisterns; Christ offers the woman at the well water springing up into everlasting life; and He promises that out of the believer's belly shall flow rivers of living water, which John says was spoken of the Spirit.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Well, a spring; a fountain; a pit dug to obtain water. Living, in Scripture, running, as living water, in distinction from stagnant. A well of living waters, Song of Solomon 4:15, the bridegroom's figure for his bride.
webster_full: Well, a spring or fountain; a pit or hole dug in the earth to obtain water.
Living, having life; of water, running or springing, not stagnant.
Hebrew be'er, a well dug or sunk to reach water beneath.
Hebrew mayim chayyim, living waters, that is, running and not still.
Required for the cleansing of the leper, Leviticus 14:5.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the figure is often spiritualized so quickly that the Song's own subject — a wife praised by her husband — disappears.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No rival doctrine attaches to the phrase. The besetting fault is a devotional one, and it runs in two directions. Some expositors move so fast to the allegory that the Song's plain subject is never allowed to stand — a bridegroom praising his own wife in terms of running water, sealed to him and cleansing — and a book God gave to sanctify marriage ends up never applied to a marriage. Others, reacting, refuse the typology altogether and leave the Song in the bedroom, as though Scripture's long use of marriage for Christ and His church began with Paul.

The principle to recover is the order the Reformed expositors kept. The literal sense comes first and is honoured: this is a husband's praise of his wife, and Christian husbands are to speak so. The typical sense is then real and not invented, because Scripture itself makes marriage the figure of Christ and the church, and the same living-water language is taken up by Christ at the well and in the temple courts, and by the LORD in Jeremiah against those who forsake the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns. Read in that order the phrase enriches both a marriage and a soul; read in either half alone it is impoverished.

word: Terrible as an Army With Banners
pronunciation: TER-uh-bul az an AR-mee with BAN-erz
pos: n. phr. (the bridegroom's figure for the awe-inspiring beauty of the bride)
etymology: Hebrew ayummah ka-nidgaloth — ayom, awful, awe-inspiring, terrible in the older English sense of causing dread; degel, a standard or banner, the plural participle meaning troops drawn up under their standards.
biblical_def: Twice the bride is described this way: “Thou art beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army with banners,” and again, “Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?” The English word terrible has shifted and now suggests what is bad; in the Authorized Version it means awe-inspiring, the same word used of the terrible day of the LORD and of the great and terrible wilderness. The figure is of ranked troops under their standards — ordered, arrayed, advancing — and the beauty being praised is therefore not a delicate thing but a commanding one that stops an onlooker where he stands. Set beside Tirzah and Jerusalem, both walled cities, the picture is of beauty with strength and order in it. Read of the church, which is how the Reformed expositors have long taken the Song's bride, the phrase is a comfort and a warning: the people of God, arrayed under their Captain's standard, are a sight before which the world has reason to be uneasy. Whether in a wife or in a congregation, Scripture here commends the beauty that is ordered, and does not treat awe and loveliness as rivals.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Terrible, adapted to excite terror or awe; dreadful; awful. Banner, a square flag; a standard; an ensign of war. Terrible as an army with banners, Song of Solomon 6:4, the awe-inspiring, ordered beauty of the bride.
webster_full: Terrible, adapted to excite terror, awe, or dread; awful; formidable.
Banner, a square flag; a military standard or ensign borne before troops.
Hebrew ayom, awful or awe-inspiring; used of the day of the LORD.
Hebrew degel, a standard or banner under which a company is ranked.

corruption_summary: The chief loss is linguistic — readers take “terrible” in its modern sense and so hear an insult where the Authorized Version intends awe.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What it faces is the ordinary hazard of an aging language. Terrible in 1611 meant awe-inspiring, as in the great and terrible wilderness and the terrible day of the LORD; today it means poor or unpleasant, so the modern ear hears the bridegroom disparaging his bride in the middle of a line of praise. The remedy is the plain one — teach the word. The Authorized Version's English is not a defect to be apologised for but a vocabulary to be learned, and this verse is a small lesson in why a congregation should be taught its Bible's words rather than hurried past them.

The second thing commonly lost is the figure's doctrine. Beauty here is ordered, arrayed, and strong — ranked troops under standards — which cuts against the modern separation of loveliness from strength and of strength from loveliness. The principle to recover is that Scripture joins them. A godly woman's adorning is a meek and quiet spirit of great price, and the same Scripture gives us the virtuous woman whose strength and honour are her clothing and whose household is in order; a faithful church is both a bride without spot or wrinkle and an army whose weapons are not carnal. The verse reproves any piety that thinks beauty must be fragile.

pos: n. phr. (the third of three exchanges the Messiah is anointed to make for mourners in Zion)
etymology: Hebrew ma'ateh tehillah — ma'ateh, a wrap or mantle, something thrown around one; tehillah, praise, the word that titles the book of Psalms in Hebrew; set against ruach kehah, the spirit of heaviness.
biblical_def: Isaiah's sixty-first chapter is the passage Christ read in the synagogue at Nazareth and claimed as fulfilled in Himself. Its third verse names three exchanges He is anointed to make for them that mourn in Zion: “to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD.” Each is a trade of a mourner's token for a festival one. Ashes were thrown on the head in grief and are swapped for an ornament; oil was left off in mourning and is given for gladness; and sackcloth, the wrapping of the bereaved, is replaced by a mantle of praise. The word rendered praise is tehillah, the Hebrew name of the Psalter, so the garment is not a mood but the thing a congregation does. Two points govern its use. The exchange is given — it is the Messiah's work for mourners, not a discipline mourners perform to qualify; and it is for those who mourn in Zion, the Lord's own afflicted people, not a general cheerfulness offered to all comers. The chapter ends with the one so clothed saying, I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, which is praise worn as a garment.

corruption_summary: The verse is turned into a technique — put on praise and the heaviness will lift — which reverses the giving and lays the exchange on the mourner instead of on the Messiah who is anointed to make it.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase has become a slogan in much charismatic and therapeutic Christian writing, where the garment is something a sufferer puts on by an act of will in order to produce a change of feeling. Isaiah's grammar runs the other way. The one anointed with the Spirit of the LORD is sent to bind up, to proclaim, and to give — the giving is His, the mourners are those appointed to receive, and the result is that they are called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He might be glorified. A command to cheer up dressed in Isaiah's language can crush an afflicted believer, which is the opposite of what the chapter was sent to do.

A second error empties the verse of its public character. Tehillah is the Psalter's own name, and a garment of praise is worn where garments are seen — in the congregation, in the singing of a gathered people, not merely in a private frame of mind. The principle to recover is the chapter's order. Christ announced in Nazareth that this scripture was fulfilled in Him; He gives the exchange, and the proper response is the sixty-first chapter's own last word, I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God — praise put on as clothing because He has clothed the wearer with the garments of salvation.

pos: n. phr. (Isaiah's answer in the temple vision, after his lips were touched)
etymology: Hebrew hinneni shelacheni — hinneni, behold me, the margin's own reading; shalach in the imperative with the first-person suffix, send me; the same hinneni answers God in the mouths of Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Jacob.
biblical_def: Isaiah sees the Lord high and lifted up, hears the seraphim cry Holy, holy, holy, and cries out that he is undone, a man of unclean lips. A seraph then takes a live coal from the altar and touches his mouth, declaring his iniquity taken away and his sin purged. Only then comes the question and the answer: “Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.” The order of the chapter is the doctrine. Vision of God's holiness, conviction of sin, atonement applied from the altar, and only after that the call and the volunteering. A man who has not seen the thrice-holy God has nothing to say in that room, and a man whose lips are unclean cannot be sent until the coal has touched them. Notice also what Isaiah was sent to: the commission immediately following is to a people whose heart is made fat and whose ears are heavy, a ministry of preaching that would mostly not be received, and he accepted it. The phrase is therefore the opposite of an eager volunteer's slogan. It is the answer of a pardoned man who has learned who God is, and who says yes before he is told the terms.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Send, to cause to go or be carried; to commission and dispatch. Here, in this place; at this point. Here am I; send me, Isaiah 6:8, the prophet's answer after the coal from the altar had touched his lips.
webster_full: Send, to cause to go or be carried; to commission and dispatch on an errand.
Here, in this place; present; at hand — the margin reads ‘behold me’.

corruption_summary: The words are detached from the chapter and used as a missions-conference slogan of willingness, with the vision, the conviction, the altar coal, and the hard commission all left out.
corruption_paragraphs: Printed on banners and sung in choruses, the phrase now most often expresses raw availability — a willing heart offering itself. Isaiah's willingness is the fifth thing in the chapter, not the first. Before he says it he has seen the Lord's train fill the temple, heard the holy cry that shook the posts of the door, pronounced himself undone, and had his mouth touched with fire from the altar. Willingness without those is enthusiasm, and the church has sent out a great many enthusiastic men who had never been undone. The call to ministry in Scripture always runs through the holiness of God and the purging of the called man's sin.

The second omission is the commission itself. The very next verses tell Isaiah to preach to a people who will hear and not understand, and he asks how long, and is told until the cities are wasted. The modern use of his words implies an expectation of visible success, which is precisely what his own sending did not include. The principle to recover is that the measure of a sent man is faithfulness and not reception. He goes because the Lord has asked who will go, and he keeps going when the hearts are fat and the ears are heavy, as Isaiah did for a lifetime and as the apostles did after him.

word: The Wolf Also Shall Dwell With the Lamb
pronunciation: thuh WOOLF AWL-soh shal DWEL with thuh LAM
pos: n. phr. (Isaiah's picture of the peace of the Messiah's reign)
etymology: Hebrew we-gar ze'eb im keves — gur, to sojourn or dwell as a guest; ze'eb, wolf; keves, a lamb; the verb is the one used of a stranger lodging peaceably in another's land.
biblical_def: After the rod out of the stem of Jesse and the Spirit resting upon Him, Isaiah describes the peace of His reign: “The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them.” Each pair sets a predator beside its natural prey, and the verb is the gentle one — the wolf sojourns with the lamb, lodging as a guest where he would have eaten. The passage gives its own ground in the ninth verse: they shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain, for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. Enmity ends because the knowledge of God fills the earth. Reformed expositors have read the picture in two complementary ways and both are in Scripture. It describes the character of Christ's kingdom already begun, where wolves are not caged but changed — Saul the persecutor becomes Paul the apostle, which is a wolf dwelling with lambs in the only way that lasts. And it looks on to the new heavens and new earth, where Isaiah repeats the words and adds that the wolf and the lamb shall feed together and dust shall be the serpent's meat. The one thing the passage will not support is a peace without the knowledge of the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Wolf, a beast of prey of the canine kind, fierce and ravenous. Lamb, the young of the sheep kind. The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, Isaiah 11:6, the peace of the Messiah's reign where the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD.
webster_full: Wolf, a beast of prey of the canine kind, fierce, ravenous, and bold.
Lamb, the young of the sheep kind; in Scripture, the figure of meekness.
Hebrew gur, to sojourn or lodge as a guest in another's place.
Hebrew ze'eb, wolf; keves, a lamb; namer, the leopard of the next clause.
Grounded in the earth full of the knowledge of the LORD, Isaiah 11:9.
scriptures: Isa 11:6

Isa 11:9

Isa 11:1
And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots:

The wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the lion shall eat straw like the bullock: and dust shall be the serpent's meat. They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: The passage is pressed into a political programme of peace without Christ, and on the other side locked into a single future millennial literalism that silences its present force.
corruption_paragraphs: Quoted at interfaith gatherings and on peace posters, the verse is regularly used to commend a reconciliation of parties that has nothing to do with the Messiah whose reign produces it. Isaiah will not be quarried that way. The chapter opens with the rod out of the stem of Jesse on whom the Spirit of the LORD rests, who judges with righteousness and smites the earth with the rod of his mouth; the peace of the sixth verse is the fruit of that Person's government, and the ninth verse names the cause as the knowledge of the LORD covering the earth. A peace sought apart from Him is the prophets' false peace, crying peace, peace, when there is no peace.

The dispensational handling errs by restricting the passage to a future earthly millennium and so removing every present claim it has on the church. Scripture itself applies Isaiah 11 to the time of the gospel: Paul quotes the eleventh chapter's root of Jesse to prove that the Gentiles now hope in Him. The Reformed reading holds both the already and the not yet — the kingdom has come in Christ and wolves are being changed now, and the full picture waits for the new heavens and new earth, where Isaiah says the same thing again. The principle to recover is that the enmity ends by conversion and consummation, not by negotiation.
roots_summary: Hebrew gur, to sojourn as a guest; ze'eb, wolf; keves, lamb — predators lodging with prey, grounded in the earth's fulness of the knowledge of the LORD.

word: Mount Up With Wings as Eagles
pronunciation: MOWNT up with WINGZ az EE-gulz
pos: v. phr. (the promise to those that wait upon the LORD, at the close of Isaiah 40)
etymology: Hebrew ya'alu ever ka-nesharim — alah, to go up or ascend; ever, a pinion or wing; nesher, the eagle; qavah, the verb rendered wait, meaning to wait with expectation, from a root of twisting or binding.
biblical_def: “But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.” The verse closes a chapter that began with comfort ye my people and has spent itself proving the incomparable greatness of God — the nations as a drop of a bucket, the heavens stretched out like a curtain, the stars brought out by number. The two verses before this one are the hinge: even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall. Human strength at its best fails; the strength promised here is God's given to those who wait. The word wait is not idling but expectant dependence, binding oneself to the LORD and looking for Him. And the order of the three clauses is often noticed and worth keeping: mounting, running, walking. It descends from flight to plodding, which is the opposite of the ascending climax a motivational reading wants, and it is the truer picture of a Christian life — there are days of soaring, days of running, and long stretches of walking without fainting, and the promise covers all three.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Mount, to rise on high; to ascend. Wait, to stay in expectation; to rest in patience. They shall mount up with wings as eagles, Isaiah 40:31, the renewing of strength promised to those that wait on the LORD.
webster_full: Mount, to rise on high; to ascend; to get up upon anything.
Wait, to stay in expectation; to look for with patience; to attend upon.
Hebrew qavah, to wait with expectation; from a root of twisting or binding.
Hebrew chalaph, to change or renew, of the strength promised.
Hebrew nesher, the eagle, noted in Scripture for height and renewed vigour.
scriptures: But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall:
He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.
Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding.
corruption_summary: The verse is detached from its chapter and sold as a promise of personal peak performance, with the waiting redefined as striving and the walking clause dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: Printed on gym walls and quoted in motivational Christian writing, the verse becomes a guarantee of personal vigour — soar higher, run harder — which inverts the chapter's argument. Isaiah has just said that the youths shall faint and the young men shall utterly fall, and the renewed strength is given to those who wait, a word of expectant dependence rather than effort. The comfort is for the exhausted and for those who think their way is hid from the LORD, and it is grounded in the everlasting God who fainteth not. A reading that turns waiting into striving offers the weary the one thing Isaiah says will fail them.

The second loss is the last clause. Preachers reach the eagles and stop, as though flight were the promise and walking a disappointment; but Isaiah ends with walking and not fainting, which is where most Christian obedience actually happens. The principle to recover is that the promise covers the ordinary. A believer in a long affliction, with no soaring in sight, is covered by the same verse as the man on the wing, and the ground of both is the same: he giveth power to the faint, and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.
roots_summary: Hebrew qavah, to wait with expectation; chalaph, to renew or exchange; nesher, eagle — and the three clauses descend from mounting to running to walking.
roots_lines: Hebrew qavah, to wait expectantly; from a root meaning to twist or bind.
Hebrew chalaph, to change, exchange, or renew — of strength renewed.
Hebrew ever, a pinion or wing; nesher, the eagle, high-flying and strong.
Hebrew ya'aph and yaga', to faint and to grow weary, denied to the waiting.
Preceded by the fainting of youths and the falling of young men, Isaiah 40:30.

pos: n. phr. (the intercessors the LORD sets over Jerusalem, charged never to hold their peace)
etymology: Hebrew shomerim al chomothayik — shamar, to keep, guard, or watch; chomah, a city wall; the charge that follows uses mazkirim, those who make mention or remind, a courtly term for the officer who brings a matter before the king.
biblical_def: “I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, which shall never hold their peace day nor night: ye that make mention of the LORD, keep not silence, and give him no rest, till he establish, and till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth.” The figure is a city wall with sentries posted on it, but the duty assigned them is not what a sentry ordinarily does. They are not told to watch for enemies; they are told to speak, and never to stop. The term used of them, those who make mention of the LORD, is the language of a court officer whose office is to keep a matter before the king until he acts. So Isaiah's watchmen are intercessors, and the LORD Himself has set them there, which is the astonishing thing in the verse: God appoints men to give Him no rest. Scripture is not embarrassed by that. Jacob wrestled and would not let go, the widow wearied the unjust judge, Moses stood in the breach, and Christ taught that men ought always to pray and not to faint. Two offices in the church draw directly from this: the preaching ministry, which Ezekiel also calls a watchman and holds accountable for warning, and the standing work of prayer, which is every believer's and is the one duty here that has no night off.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Watchman, one set to guard a city or camp; a sentinel. Wall, a work of stone or brick raised for defence. I have set watchmen upon thy walls, Isaiah 62:6, the intercessors God appoints and charges never to be silent.
webster_full: Watchman, one set to keep guard over a city, camp, or house; a sentinel.
Wall, a structure of stone or brick raised for enclosure or defence.
Hebrew shamar, to keep, guard, or watch over a charge committed to one.
Hebrew mazkirim, those who make mention; a court term for bringing a suit before the king.
Charged to give him no rest till he make Jerusalem a praise, Isaiah 62:7.
scriptures: Isa 62:6
I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, which shall never hold their peace day nor night: ye that make mention of the LORD, keep not silence,
Isa 62:7
And give him no rest, till he establish, and till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth.
Eze 33:7
So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me.

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
corruption_summary: The phrase is taken up as a title of self-appointed authority, or narrowed to political vigilance, when Isaiah's watchmen are appointed by God and their assigned work is unceasing intercession.
corruption_paragraphs: In much charismatic and prophetic-movement writing “watchman” has become a self-conferred office, a title a man takes to license pronouncements over churches and nations without ordination, examination, or accountability. Isaiah's first clause forbids it: I have set watchmen. The appointing is the LORD's, and the New Testament names the way He does it — elders ordained in every city, examined against a list of qualifications, watching for souls as they that must give account. A man who claims the wall without the church's call has claimed a post God did not give him.

A second narrowing turns the watchman into a purely political sentinel, so that the office becomes commentary on the nation's affairs. Ezekiel does give the watchman a warning ministry and holds him responsible for the blood of the unwarned, and preaching that never warns is unfaithful. But Isaiah's charge here is specific and it is prayer: make mention of the LORD, keep not silence, give him no rest. The principle to recover is that the first work on the wall is intercession, kept up day and night, until He make Jerusalem a praise in the earth — and that this is a work the whole church may do, not a title a few may wear.

pos: n. phr. (the straitened portion the Lord gives, named with the water of affliction)
etymology: Hebrew lechem tsar — lechem, bread; tsar, straitness, narrowness, distress; the pair with mayim lachats, water of oppression, is the prisoner's ration, the scant fare of a man under pressure.
biblical_def: “And though the Lord give you the bread of adversity, and the water of affliction, yet shall not thy teachers be removed into a corner any more, but thine eyes shall see thy teachers: And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it.” The phrase is the prisoner's ration — scant bread and short water, the fare Ahab ordered for Micaiah — and the first thing to mark is who serves it. Though the Lord give you: adversity here is not an accident befalling the people but a portion handed to them by God. The second thing is what is promised in the same breath. The affliction is not removed, and no relief is offered; instead the teachers are restored to sight and a voice is given behind them directing their steps. God's answer to the hard portion is His word and His instruction, which is exactly the answer the New Testament gives when it says that chastening is the Father's dealing with sons and yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness. The verse before it says the LORD waits to be gracious and that blessed are all they that wait for him; the verse after describes idols cast away. A straitened believer with his teachers before him and a word behind him has what Isaiah calls blessedness, though his bread is short.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Adversity, an event or series of events which oppose success or desire; misfortune; affliction. Bread, food in general; sustenance. The bread of adversity, Isaiah 30:20, the scant portion the Lord Himself gives, answered by teachers restored and a word behind.
webster_full: Adversity, an event or series of events opposing success; affliction; distress.
Bread, food made of grain; in Scripture, sustenance or daily portion.
Hebrew tsar, straitness, narrowness, distress — hence scant bread.
Hebrew lachats, oppression or pressure; the water of affliction beside it.
Compare the prison ration ordered for Micaiah, 1 Kings 22:27.
scriptures: And though the Lord give you the bread of adversity, and the water of affliction, yet shall not thy teachers be removed into a corner any more, but thine eyes shall see thy teachers:
And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left.

And therefore will the LORD wait, that he may be gracious unto you, and therefore will he be exalted, that he may have mercy upon you: for the LORD is a God of judgment: blessed are all they that wait for him.
Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.
corruption_summary: Adversity is reassigned to chance, to the devil, or to the sufferer's own failure of faith, and the verse's plain subject — the Lord who gives it — is removed.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teaching cannot say this verse. On that scheme hardship is always the enemy's work or the believer's unbelief, never a portion served by God; and so a Christian in a long trouble is told to rebuke what Isaiah says the Lord has handed him. Scripture's own range is wider and more comfortable: the LORD kills and makes alive, forms the light and creates darkness, and does not afflict willingly but does afflict. Job received evil as well as good from the same hand and sinned not with his lips. Naming God as the giver of the hard portion is what makes patience possible, for a portion from a Father can be borne where a random misfortune cannot.

The opposite error is fatalism, which hears the giving and stops, leaving a believer resigned under a hand he does not love. The verse itself refuses that: the sentence does not end with the bread, it ends with the teachers in sight and a word behind the ear saying, This is the way, walk ye in it. The principle to recover is the Reformed doctrine of chastening. Affliction is fatherly, measured, and purposeful; God's customary provision in it is not escape but instruction, so the straitened Christian is to look for his teachers and listen for the word rather than wait for the bread to improve.
roots_summary: Hebrew lechem tsar, bread of straitness; mayim lachats, water of oppression — the prisoner's ration, given by the Lord and answered with teachers and a guiding word.

Followed by a word behind the ear: This is the way, Isaiah 30:21.
